It uses a two-dimensional attained service\index{Attained Service Scheduling!two-dimensional}[^fn-attained-service-scheduling] scheduler that makes priority decisions based on what a job has already consumed, not what it claims it will consume. Jobs accumulate "service" based on GPU-time consumed, with priority decreasing as service increases. The two dimensions are time (how long the job has been running) and resources (how many GPUs the job uses), capturing both elapsed duration and resource intensity.

[^fn-attained-service-scheduling]: **Attained Service Scheduling**\index{Attained Service Scheduling!queueing discipline}: A discipline from OS queuing theory where priority decreases with cumulative resource consumption, approximating the theoretically optimal shortest remaining processing time (SRPT) policy without requiring the future knowledge that SRPT demands. In ML clusters, this approximation is particularly effective because job durations are heavy-tailed: the majority of submitted jobs are short experiments, so deprioritizing high-service jobs correctly identifies the long-running outliers without requiring users to provide runtime estimates they cannot accurately compute.

A discretized version groups jobs into service bins (for example, less than 1 GPU-hour, 1 to 10 GPU-hours, 10 to 100 GPU-hours, greater than 100 GPU-hours), promoting jobs in lower bins to the front of the queue. This bin structure means that all short jobs (the majority of submitted work) receive high priority and run quickly, while the few long jobs that consume most cluster resources gradually lose priority and are deprioritized relative to new arrivals. Because jobs that have consumed little service are statistically likely to be short, prioritizing them approximates SRPT and reduces average completion time without any runtime estimate.

The Tiresias evaluation reports lower average job completion times on its testbed and trace-driven workloads [@gu2019tiresias]. The result depends on job arrivals, sizes, and the comparison policy. Prioritizing low-service jobs can delay long-running jobs, so average completion time must be evaluated alongside starvation prevention and the delay experienced by each job class.

### Gandiva iteration-aware scheduling {#sec-fleet-orchestration-gandiva}

**Gandiva**\index{Gandiva!definition} [@xiao2018gandiva] exploits iteration-boundary time slicing, enabling higher utilization through controlled oversubscription. Idle portions of one job can leave execution opportunities for another, but admitting additional jobs also requires compatible memory demand, isolation, and measured switching cost; idle time alone does not establish a safe overcommit ratio. The critical insight that makes this practical is that iteration boundaries provide natural preemption points where GPU state is minimal. Between iterations, only model weights and optimizer state reside on the GPU; the intermediate activations from forward and backward passes have been freed. Releasing temporary activations reduces the state involved in a switch, although weights and optimizer state can still make switching expensive. The scheduler must measure the transition cost for the actual model and runtime.

Gandiva also implements **grow-shrink elasticity**\index{Grow-Shrink Elasticity!definition} at a finer granularity than the framework-level elastic training discussed in @sec-fleet-orchestration-elastic-training. Gandiva automatically adjusts data parallelism degree based on real-time resource availability, using profiled iteration times to predict the throughput impact of adding or removing workers. When a high-priority job arrives, Gandiva shrinks lower-priority jobs by reducing their worker count rather than killing them entirely, preserving their progress while freeing resources. When resources become available again, it grows jobs back to their preferred parallelism degree. This fine-grained elasticity, informed by actual iteration-level profiling data, enables scheduling decisions that general-purpose systems cannot make because they lack visibility into job internals.

### Themis finish-time fairness {#sec-fleet-orchestration-themis}

Traditional fair-share scheduling treats all GPU-seconds equally, even when equal shares produce very different completion delays. **Themis**\index{Themis!definition} [@mahajan2020themis] instead measures fairness in normalized finish time: each job compares its completion time under contention with the completion time it would receive under an isolated fair share of the cluster.

Themis allocates resources to improve the worst finish-time fairness ratio across jobs. A job close to completion may receive more resources when a short delay would inflate its normalized finish time more than the same allocation change would affect another job. Waiting does not waste the GPU-hours already consumed; it delays when their result becomes available. The metric therefore compares completion delay, not sunk compute, and prevents a policy from appearing fair merely because it eventually equalizes GPU-seconds.

This approach benefits shorter jobs and nearly-complete jobs without excessive penalty to longer ones, and it aligns scheduling decisions with the economic value of completing work rather than the simple accounting of resource consumption. Themis implements this metric through an auction mechanism where jobs bid for resources based on their current marginal value (how much their completion time improves per GPU-hour allocated), creating a market-like dynamic that naturally directs resources to their highest-value use.

### Pollux adaptive resource allocation {#sec-fleet-orchestration-pollux}

**Pollux**\index{Pollux!definition} [@qiao2021pollux] takes the most aggressive approach of the four research schedulers by jointly optimizing resource allocation and training hyperparameters. Where Tiresias, Gandiva, and Themis make scheduling decisions about jobs (when to run, how to share), Pollux makes decisions within jobs (how many GPUs and what batch size). The key observation is that the optimal number of GPUs for a training job depends on the current batch size, learning rate, and gradient noise level, all of which change during training as the model moves through different phases of convergence.

Pollux dynamically adjusts each job's GPU allocation and batch size to maximize cluster-wide goodput\index{Goodput!cluster-wide}, defined as the rate of useful training progress across all jobs simultaneously. The goodput metric folds both sides of the trade-off into one number: statistical efficiency (how much each gradient step advances convergence, which depends on batch size) and system throughput (how many gradient steps per second, which depends on GPU count and communication overhead). A job experiencing diminishing returns from its current GPU count (because communication overhead is growing superlinearly) may have GPUs reassigned to a job that would benefit more (because additional workers improve system throughput without an offsetting loss in statistical efficiency at the selected batch size).

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: lego-pollux-reported-jct
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ POLLUX REPORTED JCT REDUCTION (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Pollux evaluation paragraph immediately below.
# │
# │ Goal: Anchor the Pollux discussion with its published headline result.
# │ Show: 37 to 50 percent lower average JCT than the compared DL schedulers.
# │ How:  Published values, held locally until Literature carries them.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_percent

class PolluxReportedJct:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    # scenario assumption: published observation, not yet in Literature.*.
    # Qiao et al. (OSDI 2021), abstract (arXiv:2008.12260): "Pollux reduces
    # average job completion times by 37-50% relative to state-of-the-art DL
    # schedulers."
    jct_reduction_lo = 0.37
    jct_reduction_hi = 0.50
    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(0 < jct_reduction_lo < jct_reduction_hi < 1, "reported reduction must be a fractional range")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────
    jct_lo_num_str = fmt(jct_reduction_lo * 100, precision=0)
    jct_hi_pct_str = fmt_percent(jct_reduction_hi, precision=0, commas=False, style="prose")
```

The Pollux evaluation reports average job completion times `{python} PolluxReportedJct.jct_lo_num_str` to `{python} PolluxReportedJct.jct_hi_pct_str` lower than the state-of-the-art deep learning schedulers it was compared against, which do not make the same combined adjustment of resources and batch size [@qiao2021pollux]. The number belongs to that testbed and trace. Its durable lesson is the coupling: an allocation can increase samples per second while reducing progress per sample. The scheduler must estimate both effects and validate completion time at the same target quality, rather than transferring a reported improvement to a different workload.

### Scheduler comparison framework {#sec-fleet-orchestration-scheduler-comparison}

Custom ML schedulers represent a progressive trade-off between implementation complexity and scheduling precision, so the comparison in @tbl-fleet-orchestration-scheduler-comparison matters as a deployment filter rather than a ranking. General-purpose schedulers see declared resources and coarse runtime metadata; these research systems add ML-specific signals such as iteration structure, elasticity, convergence phase, and measured goodput.

| **Scheduler** | **Key Insight**                       | **Scheduling Signal**  | **Optimization Target**  | **Integration Requirement**                    |
|:--------------|:--------------------------------------|:-----------------------|:-------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------|
| **Tiresias**  | Attained service informs priority     | GPU-hours consumed     | Minimize average JCT     | Resource accounting and queue reprioritization |
| **Gandiva**   | Iteration boundaries enable sharing   | Iteration timing       | Improve utilization      | Runtime profiling and coordinated time slicing |
| **Themis**    | Completion delay defines fairness     | Normalized finish time | Improve worst fairness   | Finish-time estimates and allocation auctions  |
| **Pollux**    | Batch size and allocation are coupled | Goodput                | Maximize cluster goodput | Runtime resizing and batch-size adaptation     |

: **Custom ML Scheduler Comparison**: A taxonomy of research schedulers based on the specific workload characteristic they exploit. Tiresias and Themis optimize for queuing metrics (job completion time, fairness) using external signals, while Gandiva and Pollux optimize for efficiency using internal profiling data. {#tbl-fleet-orchestration-scheduler-comparison}

The table separates policies by what the platform must observe and control. Attained-service scheduling can work from accounting records, while iteration-aware sharing needs reliable timing profiles. Adaptive goodput policies require the training loop to accept allocation and batch-size changes. Additional control creates additional failure modes: inaccurate profiles can increase interference, and inaccurate learning-progress models can choose allocations that fail to improve convergence.

For our 175B parameter model, the practical distinction is whether the runtime supports those interventions at an acceptable transition cost. A policy that only changes queue priority needs less training-loop integration than one that resizes the execution group. The production discussion that follows evaluates that integration against the fleet's topology and recovery requirements.

The common lesson is to match the policy signal to the scheduling objective. Attained service addresses runtime uncertainty, iteration boundaries expose cheaper opportunities to interrupt work, normalized finish time measures unequal delay, and goodput couples resource allocation to learning progress. These signals support different decisions; they do not imply that every scheduler predicts convergence or makes preemption inexpensive. A platform should test the chosen policy against queue delay, starvation risk, and measured recovery cost before adopting it.

The challenge for production systems is incorporating these insights while maintaining the operational reliability, policy flexibility, and organizational governance that production environments require. Production platforms usually adopt scheduler ideas selectively because reliability, governance, heterogeneous hardware, and user policy constrain pure research designs.

### From research to production {#sec-fleet-orchestration-research-to-production}

Research schedulers become useful in production only when their core signal survives contact with a heterogeneous data center. In research, the cluster is often assumed to be a homogeneous pool of accelerators with uniform interconnect topology, and jobs are well-behaved entities that declare their resource needs accurately. In production, the "cluster" is a geological formation of hardware generations: V100s alongside A100s and H100s, connected by a patchwork of InfiniBand and Ethernet, running jobs that frequently crash, hang, or misrepresent their memory requirements. Deploying a research policy therefore requires integrating its decisions with admission, failure recovery, and the existing orchestrator; the policy alone is not a complete production control plane.

Consider our 175B-parameter model training run. A pure implementation of Pollux might aggressively resize the job based on global cluster load, scaling the number of GPUs up and down to maximize goodput. For a framework that resizes through checkpoint and restart, changing the worker count can require persisting and restoring large optimizer state. Frameworks with other state-transfer mechanisms have different transition costs. If the re-scaling interval is too short, the I/O overhead of checkpointing negates the throughput gains. One possible policy is to permit resizing while allocations change frequently and retain a stable placement when the measured transition cost outweighs the expected benefit. The appropriate boundary follows the workload and cluster demand, not a universal training phase.

The production decision is whether a specialized policy improves marginal allocation enough to justify its operational burden. This chapter evaluates that decision through queue delay, useful GPU-hours, preemption tax, and placement efficiency.

The risk is not only implementation cost; scheduler behavior can also fail to match the execution semantics of distributed training.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: lego-openai-k8s-scale
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ OPENAI KUBERNETES SCALE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: War story "OpenAI's gang-scheduling deadlock (2021)" below.
# │
# │ Goal: Pin the reported Kubernetes node count to Literature.FleetOperations.
# │ Show: 7,500 nodes.
# │ How:  Literature.FleetOperations.OpenAiKubernetesNodes.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Literature
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt

class OpenAiK8sScale:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    nodes = float(Literature.FleetOperations.OpenAiKubernetesNodes)
    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(nodes > 1000, "war story describes a multi-thousand-node cluster")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────
    nodes_str = fmt(nodes, precision=0)
```

::: {#ws-fleet-orchestration-openai-gang-scheduling .callout-war-story title="OpenAI's gang-scheduling deadlock (2021)"}

**Context**: OpenAI scaled Kubernetes clusters to `{python} OpenAiK8sScale.nodes_str` nodes for workloads including GPT-3, CLIP, and DALL-E. Their large training jobs used MPI-style execution, where all workers in a group had to be scheduled simultaneously before training could make progress [@sigler2021openai_kubernetes].

**Mechanism**: Default Kubernetes scheduling placed pods incrementally without all-or-nothing constraints. When two large experiments requested cluster capacity, Kubernetes scheduled half of each job's pods across nodes.

**Impact**: Both training jobs stalled indefinitely while holding allocated GPUs, producing zero training progress and deadlocking cluster resources.

**Fix**: OpenAI adopted a coscheduling scheduler plugin that admits a job's pods only when the whole group can be placed.

**Systems lesson**: Distributed ML scheduling must encode the job's execution semantics. For MPI-style training, "some pods scheduled" is not partial progress; it is wasted allocation. Production schedulers need gang scheduling, quota controls, and workload-aware policies rather than generic pod placement alone.

:::

A scheduler designed for general-purpose pod placement will mishandle workloads that require gang semantics, and adding gang awareness alone does not resolve priority conflicts among competing training jobs. Each of the four research schedulers examined in this section addresses one facet of this problem (runtime estimation, iteration-boundary preemption, fairness across finish times, or joint resource-hyperparameter tuning), but none addresses all facets simultaneously. The design space is therefore a set of explicit trade-offs rather than a single optimal policy.

::: {#chk-fleet-orchestration-custom-scheduler-design-space .callout-checkpoint title="Custom scheduler design space"}

Consider the trade-offs between the four research schedulers:

- [ ] **Estimate-free scheduling**: identify the information Tiresias sacrifices by eliminating runtime estimates, and describe when that sacrifice hurts scheduling quality.
- [ ] **Time-slicing limits**: identify workloads for which Gandiva's iteration-boundary time-slicing fails, and explain why.
- [ ] **Job starvation**: assess whether Themis's preference for nearly complete jobs can starve long-running pretraining jobs indefinitely.
- [ ] **Goodput-model risk**: describe the failure mode when Pollux's goodput model is wrong.

:::

The training policies just compared balance completion time, fairness, utilization, and learning progress. Serving adds a different deadline: capacity must be ready before an arriving request exhausts its latency budget. That requirement makes provisioning delay and burst headroom central to how the fleet allocates capacity to serving.

## Serving Capacity in the Shared Fleet {#sec-fleet-orchestration-serving}

When an e-commerce platform launches a major sale, requests can arrive faster than its serving replicas can process them. A training job may tolerate waiting in the admission queue; a serving request misses its deadline while additional capacity is still starting. To the fleet orchestrator, serving is therefore a claim on accelerators that must be honored quickly and that competes with training gangs for the same devices.

The orchestrator's unit is the serving replica, a ready execution group with a loaded model that may occupy one accelerator, a device partition, or a multi-accelerator gang. A 175B-parameter model may make an eight-GPU tensor-parallel group the schedulable replica, and Archetype B (DLRM at Scale) imposes the same constraint through its embedding tables: a replica whose tables are sharded across several accelerators can serve only when every shard is placed. Each replica has a measured request-processing capacity at a specified workload mix and latency target, and that measured capacity is the quantity the orchestrator uses to size and place replicas. It decides how many such groups exist, where they reside, how they are protected from interference, and which lower-priority allocations yield when serving demand grows. Language models add a memory dimension to the claim. Each in-progress response retains per-token attention state, the key-value (KV) cache, whose footprint grows with context length and concurrency even though the weights stay fixed, so a replica can exhaust its memory before it exhausts its compute.

How many replicas to run at each moment is a control problem with its own signals and delays. Accelerator utilization is a poor proxy for serving load, loading tens or hundreds of gigabytes of weights makes new replicas slow to start, and demand must therefore be anticipated rather than chased; @sec-inference-scale-autoscaling-capacity-control develops that control loop. The consequence for the orchestrator holds whatever policy the autoscaler uses: serving capacity rises and falls on timescales of minutes to hours, and every replica it adds must come from devices that training gangs could otherwise hold. Three fleet-level questions follow, namely how serving workloads share devices without interfering, when sharing pays for itself, and where the boundary between training and serving pools should sit.

### Resource isolation {#sec-fleet-orchestration-resource-isolation}

When multiple inference workloads share physical hardware, noisy-neighbor contention arises whenever one workload's resource consumption degrades another's execution speed. On GPUs, this interference manifests through four primary physical channels: memory bandwidth, cache hierarchy, host-device interconnects, and thermal dissipation. Saturated HBM interfaces throttle throughput for memory-bound kernels, while contending working sets evict lines from the shared L2 cache, degrading hit rates for colocated models. Concurrently, simultaneous host-to-device transfers compete for shared PCIe bus bandwidth, delaying tensor staging. Finally, aggregate power dissipation can trigger thermal throttling, depressing core clocks across every workload sharing the silicon. For latency-sensitive inference, even minor contention across any of these paths can inflate tail latency past acceptable service-level objectives, turning a seemingly well-provisioned cluster into an SLO-violating deployment.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: lego-mig-partition-fit
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ MIG PARTITION FIT (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: MIG placement-constraint paragraph immediately below.
# │
# │ Goal: Show internal fragmentation when a workload falls between MIG sizes.
# │ Show: a 15 GB workload wastes 5 GB on 2g.20gb and cannot fit on 1g.10gb.
# │ How:  A100 mig_profiles gpu_memory (branded GB, as in the MIG table).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Hardware
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_memory_capacity

class MigPartitionFit:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    _mig = {p.name: p for p in Hardware.Cloud.A100.mig_profiles}
    fit_gb = _mig["2g.20gb"].gpu_memory.to(GiB).magnitude  # branded size, as in the MIG table
    small_gb = _mig["1g.10gb"].gpu_memory.to(GiB).magnitude
    need_gb = 15  # scenario assumption: workload memory need
    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────
    waste_gb = fit_gb - need_gb
    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(small_gb < need_gb < fit_gb, "workload must fall between the two profile sizes")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────
    need_str = fmt_memory_capacity(need_gb * GB, unit=GB, precision=0)
    waste_str = fmt_memory_capacity(waste_gb * GB, unit=GB, precision=0)
    fit_str = fmt_memory_capacity(fit_gb * GB, unit=GB, precision=0)
    small_str = fmt_memory_capacity(small_gb * GB, unit=GB, precision=0)
```

MIG sits at the strong resource-isolation end of this design space. @Tbl-fleet-orchestration-mig-profiles already showed the fixed profiles; the operational implication is that hardware partitioning reduces cross-workload interference but turns partition choice into a placement constraint. MIG is available on supported MIG-capable NVIDIA data-center GPUs, profiles may require draining affected workloads before reconfiguration, and fixed partition sizes may not match workload requirements. A workload that needs `{python} MigPartitionFit.need_str` of GPU memory wastes `{python} MigPartitionFit.waste_str` on a `{python} MigPartitionFit.fit_str` MIG instance or cannot fit on a `{python} MigPartitionFit.small_str` instance.

Software approaches to isolation provide more flexibility at the cost of weaker guarantees. Efficiently sharing GPUs for inference requires navigating a hierarchy of isolation mechanisms, each trading performance for security. At the simplest level, **CUDA time-slicing**\index{CUDA Time-Slicing!definition} allows multiple processes to share a GPU by context-switching the compute resources. While flexible, it offers weak performance isolation because contexts compete for the entire device over time. NVIDIA's Multi-Process Service (MPS)\index{MPS!GPU sharing}[^fn-mps-gpu-sharing] allows kernels and memory copies from different processes to overlap, reducing context-switch overhead and improving utilization when one process cannot fill the device [@nvidiaCudaMps]. On Volta and newer GPUs, each MPS client has a distinct GPU virtual address space, but the clients still share execution engines, caches, memory bandwidth, and portions of the MPS fault domain. Address-space separation therefore does not imply the performance or fault isolation provided by MIG.

GPU memory accounting must still prevent one model from consuming capacity reserved for another. A distinct virtual address space blocks direct addressing of another client's allocations, but it does not create a fixed memory-capacity partition. Without enforceable per-client limits, a memory leak or unexpectedly large batch can exhaust shared device memory and disrupt colocated workloads. MPS therefore fits mutually trusting workloads whose aggregate memory footprint and interference have been measured; MIG or full-device assignment fits stronger trust and predictability requirements.

[^fn-mps-gpu-sharing]: **CUDA MPS (Multi-Process Service)**\index{MPS!GPU sharing}: NVIDIA's client-server runtime multiplexes CUDA processes through shared GPU scheduling resources. Volta and newer clients receive distinct GPU virtual address spaces, while compute, cache, bandwidth, and device-memory capacity remain shared. Fatal faults are contained only to the subset of clients sharing the affected GPU through the same MPS server, so MPS is not equivalent to a hardware partition or full-device isolation [@nvidiaCudaMps].

At the CPU level, core pinning assigns specific CPU cores to inference pods, preventing the Linux scheduler from migrating processes between cores in ways that invalidate processor caches. For latency-sensitive workloads, isolating cores using `isolcpus` kernel parameters and `taskset` affinity removes OS scheduling jitter that manifests as random latency spikes. Combined with NUMA-aware[^fn-numa-node-inference] placement, CPU affinity can reduce interference and avoid unnecessary remote-memory traffic. The tail-latency benefit depends on the host topology and request path. For a request path limited by host-memory access, cache eviction, remote NUMA access, and address-translation misses can increase tail latency. CPU placement addresses those costs only when they lie on the critical path.

[^fn-numa-node-inference]: **NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access)**\index{NUMA!inference latency}: Host-memory latency and bandwidth depend on which socket owns the memory and where the accelerator's PCIe connection terminates. CPU, memory, and device placement should therefore be evaluated together; a remote allocation can add inter-socket traffic, but its end-to-end inference penalty must be measured for the workload.

The isolation techniques discussed here represent a spectrum from stronger resource partitioning (MIG) to flexible software sharing (MPS and time-slicing), and the choice depends on the trust boundary between colocated workloads. MIG does not by itself create a complete external-tenant security boundary. A multi-tenant platform must combine device partitioning with VM or container isolation, IOMMU configuration, driver and runtime hardening, authentication and authorization, and network and storage controls. Single-organization workloads with a narrower trust boundary can use MPS or time-slicing when weaker fault and performance isolation is acceptable.

### GPU sharing economics {#sec-fleet-orchestration-gpu-sharing}

The decision to co-locate multiple models on a single GPU defines the efficiency frontier of an inference fleet. This choice operates on a spectrum: at one end, **exclusive access**\index{Exclusive Access!definition} provides device-resource isolation but strands capacity; at the other, **aggressive sharing**\index{Aggressive Sharing!definition} (via MPS or time-slicing) maximizes utilization but risks latency interference. Exclusive device assignment still depends on the surrounding host, driver, identity, network, and storage controls for tenant security. The physics of the packing trade-off are dictated by memory fragmentation and compute contention.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: lego-gpu-sharing-density
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ GPU SHARING DENSITY (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Sharing margin note and the MIG/MPS density prose immediately below.
# │
# │ Goal: Size the dark HBM left by exclusive, MIG 3g.40gb, and two-tenant MPS
# │       hosting of a 7B model on one 80 GB A100; size 175B FP16 weights.
# │ Show: 14 GB weights, 26 GB footprint, 54 GB (67.5%) dark, ~35% dark under
# │       MIG and MPS, 350 GB for 175B weights -> at least 5 A100s.
# │ How:  Llama2_7B / GPT3 parameters x FP16; A100 capacity and 3g.40gb profile
# │       in branded GB (as in the MIG table).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import Hardware, Models
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_memory, fmt_memory_capacity, fmt_params, fmt_percent

class GpuSharingDensity:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    a100_mem = Hardware.Cloud.A100.memory.capacity.to(GiB).magnitude * GB  # branded decimal GB
    mig3g_mem = {p.name: p for p in Hardware.Cloud.A100.mig_profiles}["3g.40gb"].gpu_memory.to(GiB).magnitude * GB
    small_model = Models.Language.Llama2_7B
    small_footprint = 26 * GB  # scenario assumption: weights + KV cache + activations
    tenants = 2  # scenario assumption: MPS tenants per GPU
    large_weights = Models.Language.GPT3.parameters * BYTES_FP16
    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────
    small_weights = small_model.parameters * BYTES_FP16
    excl_dark = a100_mem - small_footprint
    excl_dark_ratio = (excl_dark / a100_mem).to("").magnitude
    mig_dark_ratio = ((mig3g_mem - small_footprint) / mig3g_mem).to("").magnitude
    shared_mem = tenants * small_footprint
    shared_dark_ratio = ((a100_mem - shared_mem) / a100_mem).to("").magnitude
    min_gpus_large = math.ceil((large_weights / a100_mem).to("").magnitude)
    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(mig_dark_ratio - shared_dark_ratio) < 0.01, "prose says MIG and MPS both leave ~35 percent dark")
    check(min_gpus_large == 5, "prose says 'at least five GPUs' for 175B FP16 weights")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────
    a100_mem_gb_str = fmt_memory_capacity(a100_mem, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    small_model_b_str = fmt_params(small_model.parameters, precision=0, commas=False)
    small_weights_gb_str = fmt_memory(small_weights, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    small_footprint_gb_str = fmt_memory_capacity(small_footprint, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    excl_dark_gb_str = fmt_memory_capacity(excl_dark, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    excl_dark_pct_str = fmt_percent(excl_dark_ratio, precision=1, style="prose")
    mig_dark_pct_str = fmt_percent(round(mig_dark_ratio, 2), precision=0, style="prose")
    shared_mem_gb_str = fmt_memory_capacity(shared_mem, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    shared_dark_pct_str = fmt_percent(round(shared_dark_ratio, 2), precision=0, style="prose")
    large_weights_gb_str = fmt_memory(large_weights, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    min_gpus_large_str = fmt(min_gpus_large, precision=0)
```

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/fleet_orchestration_sharing_fill.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two stacked bars of an 80 GB GPU's memory. Exclusive hosting: a 26 GB blue used segment and a wide gray dark segment. Shared hosting: a 52 GB blue used segment and a narrow gray dark segment. Sharing reclaims the dark capacity."}

*Sharing packs two tenants, cutting wasted memory from `{python} GpuSharingDensity.excl_dark_pct_str` to `{python} GpuSharingDensity.shared_dark_pct_str`.*
:::

Consider an `{python} GpuSharingDensity.a100_mem_gb_str` A100 GPU serving a `{python} GpuSharingDensity.small_model_b_str` parameter model. The model weights in FP16 consume approximately `{python} GpuSharingDensity.small_weights_gb_str`. With a typical KV cache and activation overhead, the total runtime footprint is roughly `{python} GpuSharingDensity.small_footprint_gb_str`. Under an exclusive access policy, this single model leaves `{python} GpuSharingDensity.excl_dark_gb_str` (`{python} GpuSharingDensity.excl_dark_pct_str`) of the GPU's high-bandwidth memory dark, a waste of silicon capital. Partitioning the GPU with MIG (for example, a `3g.40gb` profile) tightens the container, reducing the waste to roughly `{python} GpuSharingDensity.mig_dark_pct_str` within the partition, but still leaves the remainder of the GPU strictly segmented. Enabling MPS to pack two such models onto the same `{python} GpuSharingDensity.a100_mem_gb_str` device consumes `{python} GpuSharingDensity.shared_mem_gb_str`, dropping the aggregate memory waste to just `{python} GpuSharingDensity.shared_dark_pct_str`. Reducing the device count also requires enough compute and bandwidth headroom to preserve throughput and latency under concurrent demand; fitting the models in memory is only the first admission condition.

This density comes at the cost of interference\index{Interference!GPU sharing}. When two workloads share a GPU via MPS, they compete for SMs and memory bandwidth. The degradation is workload-dependent: two compute-bound models (for example, large batch processing) contend for the same SMs, so each loses throughput to the other. A compute-bound model co-located with a memory-bound model (for example, decoding-heavy generation) usually interferes far less, because the two bottleneck on different hardware resources. The size of either penalty must be measured for the actual pair before the scheduler counts on the density. The scheduler's job thus becomes a multi-dimensional bin packing problem: finding complementary workloads that maximize density while respecting latency SLOs.

For a heterogeneous fleet, this logic dictates a bifurcated strategy. Our 175B parameter model requires about `{python} GpuSharingDensity.large_weights_gb_str` just for FP16 weights; on `{python} GpuSharingDensity.a100_mem_gb_str` A100s that means at least `{python} GpuSharingDensity.min_gpus_large_str` GPUs before KV cache, activation buffers, runtime workspace, and tensor-parallel granularity are included. In practice, an 8-GPU tensor-parallel replica is the cleaner scheduling unit and is a candidate for exclusive access. Conversely, the dozens of 1B to 7B parameter support models, such as toxicity classifiers, query embedding encoders, and auxiliary generation models, are prime candidates for sharing. Packing these smaller models onto shared "utility nodes" liberates high-performance clusters for the heavy lifting of foundation model inference.

```{python}
#| echo: false

# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ GPU SHARING ROI (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: callout-notebook "GPU Sharing ROI"
# │
# │ Goal: Compare exclusive vs shared GPU hosting for inference fleets.
# │ How: Pack 2 small models per GPU; compute savings in GPUs and dollars.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_count, fmt_int, fmt_memory, fmt_memory_capacity, fmt_params, fmt_qty_int, fmt_usd

class GpuSharingRoi:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    n_small = 100
    small_footprint = GpuSharingDensity.small_footprint  # same 7B serving footprint as the density prose
    n_large = 10
    large_footprint = Models.Language.GPT3.parameters * BYTES_FP16  # 175B FP16
    # nameplate magnitude in decimal GB: the model footprints in this
    # scenario are decimal, so utilization must share their unit space
    a100_mem = Hardware.Cloud.A100.memory.capacity.to(GiB).magnitude * GB
    gpus_per_large = 8
    models_per_gpu_shared = 2
    gpu_rate = Infrastructure.Pricing.Fleet.GpuHourRef.rate.to(USD / hour).magnitude
    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────
    excl_small_gpus = n_small
    excl_total_mem = excl_small_gpus * a100_mem
    excl_used_mem = n_small * small_footprint
    excl_util_pct = (excl_used_mem / excl_total_mem).to("").magnitude * 100
    excl_large_gpus = n_large * gpus_per_large
    excl_total = excl_small_gpus + excl_large_gpus
    shared_small_gpus = n_small // models_per_gpu_shared
    shared_mem_per_gpu_q = models_per_gpu_shared * small_footprint
    shared_util_pct = (shared_mem_per_gpu_q / a100_mem).to("").magnitude * 100
    shared_total = shared_small_gpus + excl_large_gpus
    saved_gpus = excl_total - shared_total
    saved_pct = saved_gpus / excl_total * 100
    annual_savings = saved_gpus * gpu_rate * HOURS_PER_YEAR
    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(excl_total == 180, f"Excl total: expected 180, got {excl_total}")
    check(shared_total == 130, f"Shared total: expected 130, got {shared_total}")
    check(abs(shared_util_pct - 65) < 1, f"Shared util: expected 65%, got {shared_util_pct}")
    check(abs(annual_savings - 876000) < 1000, f"Savings: expected ~876K, got {annual_savings}")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────
    gs_excl_util_str = fmt_percent(excl_util_pct / 100, precision=1, style='prose')
    gs_excl_total_mem_gb_str = fmt_memory_capacity(excl_total_mem, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    gs_excl_large_str = fmt_count(excl_large_gpus, label="GPU")
    gs_excl_total_str = fmt_count(excl_total, label="GPU")
    gs_shared_gpus_str = fmt_count(shared_small_gpus, label="GPU")
    gs_shared_mem_gb_str = fmt_memory_capacity(shared_mem_per_gpu_q, unit=GB, precision=0)
    gs_shared_util_str = fmt_percent(round(shared_util_pct) / 100, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    gs_shared_total_str = fmt_count(shared_total, label="GPU")
    gs_saved_gpus_str = fmt(saved_gpus, precision=0)
    gs_saved_pct_str = fmt_percent(saved_pct / 100, precision=1, style='prose')
    gs_annual_usd_str = fmt_usd(annual_savings, precision=0)
    gs_small_model_b_str = fmt_params(Models.Language.Llama2_7B.parameters, precision=0, commas=False)
    gs_large_model_b_str = fmt_params(Models.Language.GPT3.parameters, precision=0, commas=False)
    gs_n_small_str = fmt(n_small, precision=0, commas=False)
    gs_a100_mem_gb_str = fmt_memory_capacity(a100_mem, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    gs_small_footprint_gb_str = fmt_memory_capacity(small_footprint, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    gs_models_per_gpu_str = fmt(models_per_gpu_shared, precision=0, commas=False)
    gs_n_large_str = fmt(n_large, precision=0, commas=False)
    gs_gpus_per_large_str = fmt_count(gpus_per_large, commas=False, label="GPU")
    gs_large_footprint_gb_str = fmt_memory(large_footprint, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    gs_gpu_hour_rate_str = fmt_usd(gpu_rate, precision=0, commas=False, per="GPU-hour")
```

::: {#nbk-fleet-orchestration-gpu-sharing-roi .callout-notebook title="GPU sharing ROI"}

Consider a fleet serving `{python} GpuSharingRoi.gs_n_small_str` distinct `{python} GpuSharingRoi.gs_small_model_b_str` models (`{python} GpuSharingRoi.gs_small_footprint_gb_str` footprint each) and `{python} GpuSharingRoi.gs_n_large_str` distinct `{python} GpuSharingRoi.gs_large_model_b_str` models (`{python} GpuSharingRoi.gs_large_footprint_gb_str` footprint each). Assume load testing has established that each proposed co-resident pair meets its throughput and tail-latency objectives with the required headroom and isolation. The example computes the resulting capacity reduction under that assumption; memory fit alone would not establish it.

**Strategy A -- exclusive access (one model per GPU)**: The `{python} GpuSharingRoi.gs_small_model_b_str` models require `{python} GpuSharingRoi.gs_n_small_str` A100 GPUs (`{python} GpuSharingRoi.gs_a100_mem_gb_str` each), achieving only `{python} GpuSharingRoi.gs_excl_util_str` memory utilization (`{python} GpuSharingRoi.gs_n_small_str` $\times$ `{python} GpuSharingRoi.gs_small_footprint_gb_str` used out of `{python} GpuSharingRoi.gs_excl_total_mem_gb_str` total). The `{python} GpuSharingRoi.gs_large_model_b_str` models require `{python} GpuSharingRoi.gs_excl_large_str` (`{python} GpuSharingRoi.gs_n_large_str` models $\times$ `{python} GpuSharingRoi.gs_gpus_per_large_str` each for tensor parallelism). Total fleet: `{python} GpuSharingRoi.gs_excl_total_str`.

**Strategy B -- mixed sharing (MPS for small, exclusive for large)**: Pack `{python} GpuSharingRoi.gs_models_per_gpu_str` models per A100 for the `{python} GpuSharingRoi.gs_small_model_b_str` models (`{python} GpuSharingRoi.gs_models_per_gpu_str` $\times$ `{python} GpuSharingRoi.gs_small_footprint_gb_str` = `{python} GpuSharingRoi.gs_shared_mem_gb_str`, well within `{python} GpuSharingRoi.gs_a100_mem_gb_str`), requiring only `{python} GpuSharingRoi.gs_shared_gpus_str` at `{python} GpuSharingRoi.gs_shared_util_str` memory utilization. The `{python} GpuSharingRoi.gs_large_model_b_str` models remain unchanged at `{python} GpuSharingRoi.gs_excl_large_str`. Total fleet: `{python} GpuSharingRoi.gs_shared_total_str`.

Sharing reduces the fleet size by `{python} GpuSharingRoi.gs_saved_pct_str` (`{python} GpuSharingRoi.gs_saved_gpus_str` fewer GPUs). At `{python} GpuSharingRoi.gs_gpu_hour_rate_str`, this saves approximately `{python} GpuSharingRoi.gs_annual_usd_str` annually in compute costs, purely through scheduling policy.

:::

### The training-serving resource boundary {#sec-fleet-orchestration-boundary}

The deepest utilization divide in the ML fleet is the wall between training and serving. Most organizations manage these as separate fiefdoms: a "Production Serving" cluster that must handle peak traffic (and sits 50 percent idle at night) and a "Research Training" cluster that is perpetually backlogged. This **static partitioning**\index{Static Partitioning!definition} is safe but economically inefficient. **Dynamic sharing**\index{Dynamic Sharing!definition} unifies these pools, but it introduces a fundamental friction: the mode-switching cost.

Repurposing a GPU from training to serving is not instantaneous. The orchestrator must checkpoint the training job (1 to 5 minutes), kill the container, launch the inference server, load the model weights from storage (2 to 10 minutes), and run warmup queries (1 to 5 minutes) to populate compilation caches. This 5-to-20-minute switching latency means GPUs cannot react to second-by-second traffic bursts. Instead, they must follow diurnal patterns.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: diurnal-gpu-shift

# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ DIURNAL GPU SHIFT (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-fleet-orchestration-training-serving-diurnal and the
# │          callout-notebook "The diurnal GPU shift".
# │
# │ Goal: Compare static partitioning vs dynamic sharing for training/serving.
# │ How: Compare active GPUs to fleet size and convert recovered capacity into annual value.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_count, fmt_int, fmt_percent, fmt_usd

class DiurnalGpuShift:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    fleet = Systems.Clusters.Training_1K.total_accelerators
    serving_peak = 400
    serving_avg = 150
    training_fixed = 618
    reclaimed = 133
    safety_buffer = 117
    gpu_rate = Infrastructure.Pricing.Fleet.GpuHourRef.rate.to(USD / hour).magnitude
    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────
    serving_reclaimable = serving_peak - serving_avg
    peak_demand = serving_peak - safety_buffer  # reservation = peak demand + surge buffer
    static_active = serving_avg + training_fixed
    static_util_pct = static_active / fleet * 100
    dynamic_active = serving_avg + training_fixed + reclaimed
    dynamic_util_pct = dynamic_active / fleet * 100
    annual_value = reclaimed * gpu_rate * HOURS_PER_YEAR * USD
    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(static_active == 768, f"Static: expected 768, got {static_active}")
    check(static_util_pct == 75, f"Static util: expected 75%, got {static_util_pct}")
    check(dynamic_active == 901, f"Dynamic: expected 901, got {dynamic_active}")
    check(round(dynamic_util_pct) == 88, f"Dynamic util: expected 88%, got {dynamic_util_pct}")
    check(serving_reclaimable - safety_buffer == reclaimed, f"Reclaimed mismatch: {serving_reclaimable - safety_buffer}")
    check(serving_avg < peak_demand < serving_peak, "peak demand must sit between the average and the reservation")
    check(serving_peak + training_fixed <= fleet, "serving reservation plus training base must fit in the fleet")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────
    ds_static_active_str = fmt(static_active, precision=0)
    ds_static_util_str = fmt_percent(round(static_util_pct) / 100, precision=0, style='prose')
    ds_dynamic_active_str = fmt(dynamic_active, precision=0)
    ds_dynamic_util_str = fmt_percent(round(dynamic_util_pct) / 100, precision=0, commas=True, style='prose')
    ds_reclaimed_str = fmt_count(reclaimed, label="GPU")
    ds_annual_usd_str = fmt_usd(annual_value, scale="M", precision=1, commas=False)
    ds_serving_peak_str = fmt_count(serving_peak, commas=False, label="GPU")
    ds_serving_avg_str = fmt_count(serving_avg, commas=False, label="GPU")
    ds_training_fixed_str = fmt_count(training_fixed, commas=False, label="GPU")
    ds_fleet_gpus_str = fmt_count(fleet, commas=True, label="GPU")
    ds_gpu_hour_rate_str = fmt_usd(gpu_rate, precision=0, commas=False, per="GPU-hour")
    ds_serving_peak_util_str = fmt_percent(serving_avg / serving_peak, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
    ds_safety_buffer_str = fmt(safety_buffer, precision=0, commas=False)
    ds_serving_reclaimable_str = fmt_count(serving_reclaimable, commas=False, label="GPU")
    ds_training_full_util_str = fmt_percent(1.0, precision=0, style='prose')
    ds_peak_demand_str = fmt_count(peak_demand, commas=False, label="GPU")
    ds_unallocated = fleet - serving_peak - training_fixed
    ds_unallocated_str = fmt_count(ds_unallocated, commas=False, label="GPU")
```

Inference traffic typically follows a "human curve": low at 3 AM, ramping up at 8 AM, peaking at 2 PM, and tapering off at 10 PM. A smart orchestrator forecasts this curve 30 minutes in advance. At 7:30 AM, it preempts low-priority training jobs (like hyperparameter sweeps) to warm up inference replicas. At 10:30 PM, as traffic drops, it drains inference replicas and releases GPUs back to the training scheduler. @Fig-fleet-orchestration-training-serving-diurnal tracks this 24-hour capacity reallocation across a `{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_fleet_gpus_str`-GPU fleet: serving demand (green) crests at `{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_peak_demand_str` mid-afternoon beneath a `{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_safety_buffer_str`-GPU hatched surge buffer, allowing the light-blue reclaim band to return an average of `{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_reclaimed_str` idle GPUs to training overnight below the `{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_serving_peak_str` static reservation line.

::: {#fig-fleet-orchestration-training-serving-diurnal fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Training vs. serving diurnal GPU capacity shift**: One day on the `{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_fleet_gpus_str` fleet of the diurnal GPU shift notebook, drawn from the same numbers. Serving demand (green) averages `{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_serving_avg_str` and peaks at `{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_peak_demand_str`; the orchestrator keeps a `{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_safety_buffer_str`-GPU surge buffer above the forecast, so the serving side never exceeds the `{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_serving_peak_str` a static partition would reserve (dashed line). Everything between the buffer and that line returns to training, averaging `{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_reclaimed_str` over the day, on top of the `{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_training_fixed_str` training base. The shape of the daily curve is illustrative; its average and peak are the notebook's." fig-alt="Stacked area chart of GPU count over 24 hours. From the bottom: green serving demand low overnight and peaking mid-afternoon, a hatched pale green surge buffer above it, a light blue band of training reclaimed from the serving reservation that is widest at night and vanishes at the afternoon peak, and a dark blue training base filling the rest of the fleet. A dashed line marks the static serving reservation at 400 GPUs."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ DIURNAL CAPACITY SHIFT (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-fleet-orchestration-training-serving-diurnal.
# │
# │ Goal: Show the notebook's dynamic-sharing policy over one day, so the
# │       figure and the notebook report the same fleet, reservation, buffer,
# │       and reclaimed capacity.
# │ Show: Stacked areas: serving demand, surge buffer, reclaimed training,
# │       training base; dashed static serving reservation.
# │ How:  Illustrative diurnal shape u(t)^2 (low near 03:00, high near 14:00),
# │       scaled so its time average and maximum equal DiurnalGpuShift's
# │       serving_avg and peak_demand; every other quantity comes from the LEGO.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
from binder.tools.figures import style as book_style

D = DiurnalGpuShift
fig, ax, COLORS, plt = book_style.setup_plot(figsize=(8, 4.2))

# ┌── 1. DEMAND CURVE (shape illustrative; mean and peak from the LEGO) ────────
t = np.linspace(0, 24, 24 * 12 + 1)
t_low, t_high = 3.0, 14.0
phase = np.where(
    t < t_low,
    np.pi + np.pi * (t + 24 - t_high) / (24 + t_low - t_high),
    np.where(t < t_high, np.pi * (t - t_low) / (t_high - t_low), np.pi + np.pi * (t - t_high) / (24 + t_low - t_high)),
)
u = ((1 - np.cos(phase)) / 2) ** 2  # time average 3/8, maximum 1
u_mean = 3 / 8
amp = (D.peak_demand - D.serving_avg) / (1 - u_mean)
base = D.peak_demand - amp
demand = base + amp * u

serving_alloc = demand + D.safety_buffer  # never exceeds the reservation
reclaimed = D.serving_peak - serving_alloc
check(np.all(serving_alloc <= D.serving_peak + 1e-9), "buffered serving must fit inside the reservation")
check(abs(np.trapezoid(reclaimed, t) / 24 - D.reclaimed) < 1.0, "figure's daily-average reclaim must match the notebook")

# ┌── 2. RENDER ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
top_train = D.serving_peak + D.training_fixed
ax.fill_between(t, 0, demand, color=COLORS['GreenLine'], alpha=0.85, lw=0, label='Serving demand')
ax.fill_between(t, demand, serving_alloc, facecolor=COLORS['GreenL'], edgecolor=COLORS['GreenLine'], hatch='///', lw=0, label='Surge buffer')
ax.fill_between(t, serving_alloc, D.serving_peak, color=COLORS['BlueL'], lw=0, label='Training on reclaimed GPUs')
ax.fill_between(t, D.serving_peak, top_train, color=COLORS['BlueLine'], alpha=0.85, lw=0, label='Training base')
ax.axhline(D.serving_peak, color=COLORS['primary'], ls='--', lw=1.1)
ax.axhline(D.fleet, color=COLORS['grid'], lw=0.8)

ax.text(
    23.6,
    D.serving_peak + 14,
    f'static serving reservation ({D.serving_peak:,} GPUs)',
    ha='right',
    va='bottom',
    fontsize=9,
    color=COLORS['primary'],
    bbox=dict(boxstyle='round,pad=0.2', facecolor='white', edgecolor='none', alpha=0.85),
)
ax.text(
    12,
    (D.serving_peak + top_train) / 2,
    f'training base: {D.training_fixed:,} GPUs',
    ha='center',
    va='center',
    fontsize=10,
    color='white',
    fontweight='bold',
)
ax.annotate(f'reclaimed for training\n(average {D.reclaimed:,})', xy=(3, 330), ha='center', va='center', fontsize=9, color=COLORS['primary'])
ax.annotate(f'serving demand\n(average {D.serving_avg:,}, peak {D.peak_demand:,})', xy=(14, 70), ha='center', va='center', fontsize=9, color='white')
ax.annotate(
    f'surge buffer ({D.safety_buffer:,})',
    xy=(20.5, float(np.interp(20.5, t, demand + D.safety_buffer / 2))),
    xytext=(20.8, 300),
    ha='center',
    va='center',
    fontsize=9,
    color=COLORS['primary'],
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='-', color=COLORS['primary'], lw=0.6),
)

ax.set_xlim(0, 24)
ax.set_ylim(0, D.fleet)
ax.set_xticks(range(0, 25, 3))
ax.set_xticklabels([f'{h:02d}:00' for h in range(0, 25, 3)])
ax.set_yticks([0, 200, D.serving_peak, 600, 800, D.fleet])
ax.set_xlabel('Time of day')
ax.set_ylabel('GPUs')
ax.grid(False)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
plt.close()
```

:::

::: {#nbk-fleet-orchestration-diurnal-gpu-shift .callout-notebook title="The diurnal GPU shift"}

Consider a fleet of `{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_fleet_gpus_str` managed under two regimes:

**Scenario A -- static partitioning**: The serving pool reserves `{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_serving_peak_str`, enough for peak demand of `{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_peak_demand_str` plus a `{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_safety_buffer_str`-GPU surge buffer, but average usage is only `{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_serving_avg_str` (`{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_serving_peak_util_str` utilization). The training pool reserves `{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_training_fixed_str`, and backlog ensures `{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_training_full_util_str` utilization. Result: `{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_serving_avg_str` + `{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_training_fixed_str` = `{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_static_active_str` active GPUs. Fleet utilization: `{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_static_util_str`. The `{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_unallocated_str` outside the serving and training reservations remain unallocated maintenance headroom in both scenarios.

**Scenario B -- dynamic sharing**: Serving holds forecast demand (average `{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_serving_avg_str`) plus the same `{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_safety_buffer_str`-GPU surge buffer. Training reclaims the rest of the serving reservation—the unused `{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_serving_reclaimable_str` on average minus the buffer, depicted by the light-blue reclaim band in @fig-fleet-orchestration-training-serving-diurnal that averages `{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_reclaimed_str` over the course of the day. Because each role switch costs minutes, the orchestrator moves this capacity on the forecast rather than chasing individual traffic spikes. Result: serving (`{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_serving_avg_str`) + training (`{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_training_fixed_str` + `{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_reclaimed_str`) = `{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_dynamic_active_str` active GPUs (the second training term is reclaimed serving capacity). Fleet utilization: `{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_dynamic_util_str`.

Dynamic sharing recovers `{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_reclaimed_str` of effective capacity. At `{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_gpu_hour_rate_str`, this creates approximately `{python} DiurnalGpuShift.ds_annual_usd_str` per year in value without purchasing a single additional accelerator.

:::

Optimizing isolation for a single deployment is straightforward, but maintaining strict guarantees becomes volatile when thousands of training and serving workloads coexist on the same infrastructure. The collision of high-priority inference SLAs with resource-hungry training jobs creates a noisy neighbor problem that simple containerization cannot solve. Multi-tenancy and quotas become the governance layer that arbitrates fair access and prevents tragedy-of-the-commons scenarios in shared fleets.

## Multi-Tenancy and Quotas {#sec-fleet-orchestration-multi-tenancy}

When the computer vision team hoards 500 GPUs for a week while the natural language processing team sits blocked trying to push a critical bug fix to production, shared clusters devolve into a tragedy of the commons. Teams with the most aggressive job submission rates, the largest jobs, or the most persistent resubmission scripts consume disproportionate resources, while teams with more modest or intermittent needs find the cluster perpetually occupied. This creates organizational friction, political escalation to management, and underinvestment in slower-moving but potentially higher-value projects whose teams lack the engineering effort to compete for resources.

Multi-tenancy and quotas provide the organizational and technical firewalls needed to prevent this degradation. The quota systems discussed here establish formal policies for resource allocation, borrowing, and reclamation, so fair access and high overall utilization become enforceable scheduler properties rather than managerial negotiation.

### Hierarchical fair-share {#sec-fleet-orchestration-fair-share-multi}

GPU quota allocation typically operates at the namespace or project level, defining how much of the cluster each team is entitled to use. The simplest approach allocates fixed GPU counts per team: Team A gets 500 GPUs, Team B gets 300 GPUs, Team C gets 200 GPUs. This approach is easy to understand and implement but leads to systematic underutilization when teams have variable workloads. If Team A's 500-GPU allocation sits 50 percent idle during a quiet period while Team B's queue overflows with urgent work, the cluster wastes 250 GPUs of capacity that rigid quotas forbid Team B from using. The alternative, allocating less quota to each team, creates a different problem: teams are blocked from running legitimate work during peak periods even when the cluster has overall spare capacity.

Hierarchical quotas separate a team's guaranteed share from its maximum permitted allocation. In @eq-fleet-orchestration-quota, $Q_{\text{team}}$ denotes that maximum cap, not the guarantee; $Q_{\text{department}}$ is the department's total capacity limit, and $U_{\text{allocated}}$ is each sibling team's current allocation. Assuming those allocations remain within the department limit, the equation gives an admission ceiling before any reclamation:

$$ Q_{\text{effective}} = \min\left(Q_{\text{team}},\ Q_{\text{department}} - \sum_{\text{other teams}} U_{\text{allocated}}\right) $$ {#eq-fleet-orchestration-quota}

The admission ceiling does not encode fair-share weights or guarantees. When demand exceeds capacity, the scheduler must also apply its fairness policy to feasible gangs. Unused guaranteed capacity can be lent within the hierarchy: if Team A uses only 60 percent of its 500-GPU allocation, the remaining 200 GPUs become available to other teams within the same department.

### Burst capacity and quota borrowing {#sec-fleet-orchestration-burst-capacity}

Lending turns unused guarantees into burst capacity. Suppose a small team holds a guarantee of 64 GPUs but needs 256 for a weekend-long training run while a sibling team's guaranteed share sits idle. The small team may borrow idle whole devices up to its maximum quota. Those devices remain part of physical cluster capacity rather than becoming virtual capacity, and they carry lower preemption priority than owned resources. When the sibling team submits work that needs its guarantee, the scheduler reclaims the borrowed devices by preempting or shrinking the borrower's opportunistic jobs.

Borrowing is what allows a multi-tenant cluster to reach high utilization. Without it, organizations face a painful choice between reserving enough quota to handle each team's peak demand, which leaves capacity idle when peaks do not coincide, and allocating less, which blocks teams during peak periods even when reclaimable capacity exists elsewhere. Borrowing provides a reclaimable entitlement subject to the platform's response-time objective, safety headroom, and current physical capacity. A team entitled to 500 GPUs can reclaim borrowed devices according to that contract, but the scheduler must not promise an immediate 500-GPU allocation when failures, nonpreemptible reservations, or recovery headroom reduce reclaimable capacity.

Burst capacity therefore expands aspirational maxima and fair-share weights, not simultaneous guarantees. The sum of guarantees that the platform promises to honor concurrently must fit reclaimable physical capacity after nonpreemptible reservations and safety headroom. Teams may advertise higher maximums or weights because borrowed jobs yield when guaranteed demand returns, but those values are not guarantees. Fractional sharing is a separate mechanism that requires an explicit MIG, MPS, or time-slicing contract.

Reclamation couples quota policy to the checkpoint infrastructure. The admission controller separates guaranteed jobs, which run on the team's owned quota and face preemption only from higher-priority work, from opportunistic jobs, which run on borrowed capacity, yield first, and must checkpoint often enough that reclamation wastes little work. Elastic jobs soften reclamation further through the graceful preemption of @sec-fleet-orchestration-elastic-scheduler-integration, shrinking toward their minimum viable allocation rather than terminating.

To govern quota borrowing safely, clusters typically establish a strict four-tier priority hierarchy. At the summit, production serving\index{Priority class!production serving} (Priority 0) workloads run nonpreemptibly to safeguard latency SLAs. Below them, production training\index{Priority class!production training} (Priority 1) workloads drive scheduled foundation-model updates and can be preempted only during severe serving failovers. Interactive and debug\index{Priority class!interactive and debug} sessions (Priority 2) receive rapid scheduling precedence to preserve engineer iteration speed, but enforce strict execution time limits to prevent resource camping. Finally, batch and research\index{Priority class!batch and research} tasks (Priority 3) execute with full preemption tolerance, consuming surplus capacity with the understanding that they yield immediately when higher-priority jobs arrive. This structured hierarchy allows large hyperparameter sweeps or exploratory experiments to fill otherwise idle capacity without risking starvation or deadline violations for business-critical jobs. Reclamation still requires the checkpointing, orderly shutdown, and readiness delays defined by each workload's contract.

The safe burst limit follows from reclaimability rather than average SM utilization. The scheduler must measure how quickly borrowed jobs can checkpoint, shrink, or terminate; reserve the I/O and network bandwidth required for that transition; and bound the amount of opportunistic capacity that can be reclaimed within the guarantee's response-time objective. A job that averages 70 percent SM activity may still reserve all device memory and require every rank in its gang, so the remaining 30 percent does not constitute an allocatable device fraction.

### Resource accounting and observability {#sec-fleet-orchestration-resource-accounting}

The 64 GPUs that sat idle for a weekend because a researcher forgot to cancel a reservation represent invisible waste in a multi-tenant cloud fleet. In a dedicated cluster, such waste is at least visible: the lights are on, but the fans are quiet. In a shared environment, the cost is hidden and compounds across thousands of jobs. Effective governance requires moving beyond simple "allocation" metrics to a tiered accounting model that distinguishes between what was requested, what was used, and what was useful.

Three tiers of measurement expose this gap between requested hardware and actual progress. Allocated capacity represents the physical resources the scheduler has reserved for a job, rendering them unavailable to competing workloads. Compute utilization measures active hardware execution, the fraction of time GPU kernels are executing instructions on silicon. Finally, productive utilization captures the proportion of allocated time that directly advances useful training or serving progress, explicitly excluding time consumed by pipeline stalls, communication barriers, data-loading starvation, and crash recovery. This distinction is operational rather than merely accounting: a team might be allocated 500 GPUs but register only 350 active devices (70 percent compute utilization) and productively advance work on just 280 (56 percent of their allocation). That 44 percent gap exposes where cluster capacity disappears, guiding targeted remediation rather than blunt quota adjustments.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol2_fleet_orchestration_margin_004.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Three horizontal orange utilization bars labeled allocated 500, active 350, and productive 280, decreasing from top to bottom."}

*Allocated, active, and productive utilization drift far apart.*
:::

Attribution in a shared fleet presents a control problem. Every admitted job needs an owner, project, workload class, and preemption contract so the scheduler can apply quota and recovery policy consistently. Kubernetes labels and Slurm accounts carry this scheduling identity.

This data feeds the utilization dashboard, the cluster operator's primary instrument for fleet health. This view must synthesize per-team utilization against quotas, queue depth by priority class, and the **fragmentation index**\index{Fragmentation Index!definition}, a measure of free GPUs that cannot be allocated due to topology constraints. It must also track preemption rates, spot interruptions, checkpoint traffic, and the recovery overhead they induce. These measurements let the scheduler distinguish idle capacity it can reclaim from allocated capacity whose apparent idleness reflects communication, I/O, or a rigid gang dependency.

Automated anomaly detection turns these metrics into actionable signals. A sudden spike in a team's consumption to 3$\times$ their historical norm might indicate a runaway script spawning infinite jobs. A queue that grows faster than it drains signals a capacity shortfall that auto-scaling must address. Conversely, a sudden drop in cluster-wide power consumption often signals a mass stall before jobs time out and fail, commonly caused by a shared dependency such as a storage outage. These alerts allow operators to intervene before the budget is drained or the queue becomes unmanageable.

::: {#psp-fleet-orchestration-three-utilization-metrics .callout-perspective title="The three utilization metrics"}

Each tier points to a different remedy. Low allocated utilization\index{Utilization!allocated} indicates missing demand or overly restrictive quotas, so the fix lies in policy. Low compute utilization\index{Utilization!compute} on allocated devices points inside the job, to inefficient code, input starvation, or communication stalls. Low productive utilization\index{Utilization!productive} despite busy kernels implicates poor distributed scaling, excessive checkpointing, or frequent restarts.

:::

### Security and namespace isolation {#sec-fleet-orchestration-security-isolation}

Multi-tenancy requires not only fair resource allocation but also security isolation that prevents teams from interfering with or observing each other's workloads. The stakes are real: ML models represent significant intellectual property, training data may contain sensitive information subject to privacy regulations, and the models themselves may encode proprietary business logic. Without proper isolation, a compromised or misconfigured workload in one team's namespace could access another team's model weights, training data, or inference traffic.

In Kubernetes environments, namespace separation provides an administrative boundary that must be reinforced by the host, device, network, and storage controls described here. Each team operates within dedicated namespaces with role-based access control limiting visibility to their own resources. Role-based policies control who can submit jobs, view logs, access model artifacts, and modify scheduling policies within each namespace, providing organizational governance over cluster usage.

Network policies extend isolation to the network layer, preventing cross-namespace communication except through explicitly permitted services. Network policies for ML workloads must balance isolation against the communication requirements of distributed training. A practical policy might permit communication among the workers of an admitted gang (ring AllReduce exchanges chunks along ring neighbors, while other algorithms use different peer patterns) while blocking all ingress from other namespaces (preventing external workloads from intercepting gradient traffic or model updates). Egress policies can prevent training jobs from accessing external networks, reducing data exfiltration risk from compromised training code or poisoned dependencies.

@Tbl-gpu-virtualization-isolation-spectrum compares GPU virtualization options across isolation strength, resource efficiency, and workload fit.

| **Option**                  | **Isolation strength**                                             | **Efficiency and flexibility**                         | **Suitable workload or trust boundary**                                    |
|:----------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Time-slicing**            | Separate contexts; shared performance and device fault domains.    | Flexible; no spatial reservation.                      | Trusted, bursty jobs.                                                      |
| **MPS**                     | Separate address spaces; shared performance and GPU fault domains. | Concurrent kernels; configurable limits.               | Mutually trusting jobs with measured demand.                               |
| **MIG**                     | Hardware-partitioned memory, cache, and compute.                   | Predictable; fixed profiles.                           | SLO-sensitive work; external tenants also need platform security controls. |
| **Full device passthrough** | Exclusive access to the GPU.                                       | Strongest device isolation; lowest packing efficiency. | Jobs that saturate the device or forbid sharing.                           |

: **GPU Virtualization Isolation Spectrum**: GPU sharing mechanisms trade device-resource isolation against packing efficiency. External tenant isolation additionally depends on the host, driver, identity, network, and storage security boundaries. {#tbl-gpu-virtualization-isolation-spectrum tbl-colwidths="[23,27,23,27]"}

The choice depends on the trust boundary between colocated workloads and the performance sensitivity of each workload type. Security in multi-tenant environments extends beyond simple resource fairness. Side-channel attacks on shared GPUs are a documented vulnerability; by monitoring contention on shared caches or memory controllers, a malicious tenant can infer the architecture or even data properties of a co-resident model. In sensitive environments, MIG or dedicated devices can strengthen device-resource isolation, but either mechanism remains one component of the larger host and platform security boundary.

### Priority preemption cascades {#sec-fleet-orchestration-preemption-cascades}

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/fleet_orchestration_preempt_cascade.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="One red source node on the left with arrows fanning out to five separate downstream nodes on the right, showing one event displacing many."}

*One eviction ripples to many: the preemption cascade.*
:::

When a high-priority job enters a saturated cluster, the scheduler must decide which running workloads to terminate to free up resources. This decision is rarely isolated. In tightly packed clusters, evicting a medium-priority job to accommodate a high-priority request often triggers a **preemption cascade**\index{Preemption Cascade!definition}, where the evicted job immediately attempts to reschedule itself by displacing lower-priority workloads. Without dampening controls, a single urgent inference service deployment can ripple through the queue, destabilizing dozens of training jobs and forcing a storm of checkpoint reloads that saturate storage bandwidth.

```{python}
#| echo: false

# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PREEMPTION TAX (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-fleet-orchestration-preemption-cascades
# │
# │ Goal: Quantify wasted cost and GPU-hours from repeated preemptions.
# │ How: Convert recovery time across all GPUs into wasted GPU-hour cost.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Systems
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_count, fmt_time, fmt_usd

class PreemptionTax:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    fleet = Systems.Clusters.Lab_64_H100
    gpus = fleet.total_accelerators
    lost_duration = 15 * minute  # scenario assumption
    reload_duration = 20 * minute  # scenario assumption
    warmup_duration = 10 * minute  # scenario assumption
    gpu_hour_rate = Infrastructure.Pricing.Fleet.GpuHourRef.rate.to(USD / hour).magnitude
    preemptions_per_day = 12  # scenario assumption
    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────
    recovery_duration = lost_duration + reload_duration + warmup_duration
    recovery_minutes = recovery_duration.to(minute).magnitude
    recovery_hours = recovery_duration.to(hour).magnitude
    cost_per_event = gpus * recovery_hours * gpu_hour_rate
    wasted_duration_per_day = preemptions_per_day * recovery_duration
    wasted_hours_per_day = wasted_duration_per_day.to(hour).magnitude
    wasted_gpu_hours_per_day = gpus * wasted_hours_per_day
    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(recovery_duration.check("[time]"), f"Expected recovery duration, got {recovery_duration}")
    check(wasted_duration_per_day.check("[time]"), f"Expected wasted duration, got {wasted_duration_per_day}")
    check(recovery_minutes == 45, f"Expected 45 minutes, got {recovery_minutes}")
    check(cost_per_event == 96, f"Expected $96, got {cost_per_event}")
    check(wasted_gpu_hours_per_day == 576, f"Expected 576 GPU-hours, got {wasted_gpu_hours_per_day}")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────
    recovery_duration_min_attr_str = fmt_time(recovery_duration, minute, precision=0, commas=False, style="word", attributive=True)
    gpu_hour_rate_str = fmt_usd(gpu_hour_rate, precision=0, commas=False, per="GPU-hour")
    cost_per_event_str = fmt_usd(cost_per_event, precision=0)
    wasted_duration_per_day_h_str = fmt_time(wasted_duration_per_day, hour, precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
    wasted_gpu_hours_per_day_str = fmt_count(wasted_gpu_hours_per_day, label="GPU-hour", plural_label="GPU-hours")
    lost_min_str = fmt_time(lost_duration, minute, precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
    reload_min_str = fmt_time(reload_duration, minute, precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
    warmup_min_str = fmt_time(warmup_duration, minute, precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
    preemptions_per_day_str = fmt(preemptions_per_day, precision=0, commas=False)
    gpus_str = fmt(gpus, precision=0, commas=False)
```

The engineering cost of preemption extends far beyond the scheduling latency. The **preemption tax**\index{Preemption Tax!definition} is the sum of lost computation since the last checkpoint, the overhead of persisting state, and the cold-start penalty upon resumption. For large-scale distributed training, every term is paid by the whole allocation. Consider the `{python} PreemptionTax.gpus_str`-GPU fine-tuning run for our 175B parameter model. If preempted, the job loses the work performed since the last snapshot (on average `{python} PreemptionTax.lost_min_str`). Upon restarting, it requires `{python} PreemptionTax.reload_min_str` to reload the optimizer state from distributed storage and another `{python} PreemptionTax.warmup_min_str` of warmup as data pipelines refill prefetch buffers, just-in-time (JIT) compilers re-optimize kernels, and GPU caches re-populate.

Reconstructing the distributed data pipeline also belongs in the preemption contract. The checkpoint must preserve the sampling and loader state needed to resume the intended data order, alongside model and optimizer state. If the restart path omits that state, it can repeat or skip samples and lose exact replay of the training trajectory. A different shuffle order does not by itself prove statistical corruption, but the recovery policy must specify which changes are acceptable. The scheduler should therefore measure restoration and pipeline warmup as part of recovery cost, rather than assume that reloading model weights alone makes the job productive.

During this `{python} PreemptionTax.recovery_duration_min_attr_str` recovery window, the GPUs are active but effectively unproductive. At `{python} PreemptionTax.gpu_hour_rate_str`, a single preemption event costs `{python} PreemptionTax.cost_per_event_str` in wasted compute capital. If the scheduler allows unlimited preemption, `{python} PreemptionTax.preemptions_per_day_str` preemptions per day waste `{python} PreemptionTax.wasted_duration_per_day_h_str` per day of that job's allocation, or `{python} PreemptionTax.wasted_gpu_hours_per_day_str` per day for this `{python} PreemptionTax.gpus_str`-GPU run. To mitigate this, schedulers enforce **preemption budgets**\index{Preemption Budgets!definition}. These rate limits constrain disruption frequency, such as preventing a job from being preempted more than once per hour or capping total cluster preemption churn to 5 percent of capacity in any 10-minute window. This forces the scheduler to wait for natural job completions rather than triggering a cascade, trading slightly higher pending times for significantly higher aggregate throughput.
